prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I withdraw the two-part configuration from round 1 and now propose a single prize part on optical lattice clocks (B024) for Katori and Ye. The reason is the chair summary's own finding on B019: Danielsson, Johansson and Kroll each say they cannot support a sole credit to Halzen for a collaboration of hundreds, and I agree with them. The scientific case for the diffuse high-energy astrophysical neutrino flux is strong, but the supplied credit omits the people who built AMANDA and IceCube, the source-level astronomy is still at about 4 to 5 sigma for a few objects, and the three-person cap leaves no room to repair this. A part I cannot defend on credit should not ride along with a part I can. B024 stands on its own. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a specific idea: a light-shift-free trap that holds very many neutral atoms Doppler- and recoil-free. The realisation by Ye and others at the 10^-18 level is reproduced in many independent laboratories and intercompared across continents, which is the kind of experimental maturity I look for as an instrument builder. The two names map exactly onto invention and realisation, with no one forced out by the three-person limit. I want the citation to name the lattice invention and the realisation, not a record accuracy figure and not the still-prospective redefinition of the second, which Lindroth and Kroll agree is a timing question and not a scientific one.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains lineage: the 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland) already recognised the comb and ion control, and a sceptic can read lattice clocks as a continuation. I answer that neutral-atom magic-wavelength trapping is a different physical idea, since it solves the light-shift problem that single-ion clocks avoid by other means, but I accept that this is a judgement and not a settled fact. The delivered physics so far is capability, with tests of constants and dark matter setting limits only; Lindroth is right about that. Ye's work spans several platforms and the early Yb and Hg lattice work could prompt questions about omissions, although I do not find a missing third name in the supplied credit. Against B044 specifically: it has the broadest support (four preferred, two first places), I have no scientific objection to the Kane-Mele Z2 classification or the HgTe experiment, and I could vote for it. My reservation is that a three-name prize cannot be defended against Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose proposal told Molenkamp's group where to look, and I would prefer the clean credit.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B044 as first choice, finds the 2016 overlap unpersuasive because Z2 insulators are a distinct symmetry-protected class, and states he cannot resolve the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap from the supplied names alone.
responses.response: I accept your distinction from 2016. A time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator with helical edge states is a different object from the quantum-Hall and Haldane-model phases, and I no longer treat overlap as a reason against B044. Our disagreement is the one you state yourself: you cannot resolve the attribution gap, and neither can I. Three of your colleagues propose wording the citation around the prediction and the HgTe quantum-well discovery, which addresses the 3D contributors but not BHZ, because the Molenkamp experiment was designed around their proposal. A prize that credits the experiment without the proposal that selected the material is the sort of allocation I would not want to defend publicly. That is why I still prefer B024, though I rate B044 as a serious second and have kept it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B044 after the openings and would restrict the citation to the Kane-Mele prediction and the HgTe quantum-well discovery, treating the missing contributors as a limit of the three-name set.
responses.response: Your restricted wording is the most defensible one on the table, and it answers the chair-summary question about the three-dimensional work. I disagree that restricting it settles the credit. If the citation is limited to the two-dimensional effect in HgTe, then the person who proposed HgTe/CdTe as the platform becomes more conspicuous by absence, not less. I also note your remark that the effect is routinely reproduced in calculations and measurements, which I take as a point of real strength for B044. Given a three-name cap, I consider a gap that sits inside the cited claim more serious than one that lies outside it, and that is the difference between our positions.

responses.point: Kroll treats lattice clocks as the clearest case of better measurement opening new physics, counts geodesy and constant tests as results the clock has opened, and calls the two-name credit complete.
responses.response: I agree with the credit and the maturity. I do not follow you on the claim that new physics has already been opened: as Lindroth says, the constant-variation and dark-matter results so far are limits, and the centimetre-scale geodesy is a demonstration of capability. For that reason I would not put those applications in the citation. Naming the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 realisation is accurate today and does not depend on what the redefinition of the second brings. Your flagged Boulder stay with Hall is a field connection, not a tie to Katori or Ye, and I see no reason it should change the weight of your support.

responses.point: Lindroth wants the citation to stress invention and realisation because delivered results on constants and dark matter are limits, and flags that Ye's multi-platform work and early Yb and Hg lattice work could prompt omission questions.
responses.response: I adopt your framing in my citation. On omissions, the question is whether the invention and the first 10^-18 realisation belong to two people. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice, and Ye's strontium clocks and intercomparisons delivered the performance the proposal promised. Early Yb and Hg work refined parameters on a route that Katori's idea had defined, so I do not see a third claim of the same standing. You and Mehlig say the 2005 and 2012 prizes make this a continuation. I part company with you there, for the reason I give above, but I acknowledge it is where B024 is most exposed.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B016) on conceptual novelty and concedes that any three-of-four allocation omits Crooks or Searles, and that the topic has no single dramatic observation.
responses.response: I agree that the conceptual standing of exact fluctuation relations is high and that the experimental record in single-molecule pulling and colloids is solid. For the allocation question you pose, my test is the same one I apply to B044 and B019: does the credit hold when the people left out are named? You have acknowledged that it does not for B016, since Crooks's detailed fluctuation theorem is close to Jarzynski's and Evans-Searles is a separate early result. A claim whose credited set you yourself describe as contestable is harder to carry than a two-name credit that no colleague has called incomplete, so I keep it behind B024.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards magic-wavelength lattice trapping as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, which is a judgement that colleagues here have split on.

Whether the attribution gap around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a limit of a three-name prize or disqualifying; I treat it as serious enough to prefer B024 but not as disqualifying B044, and four colleagues weigh it differently.

I rely on my recollection of the priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and parallel ideas, and of the 4 to 5 sigma source significances for IceCube; I have not verified either independently.
Whether the timing of the redefinition of the second, which has not yet happened, should affect when a lattice-clock prize is awarded; I regard it as a timing question and not a scientific one.
statement.conflict_note: No documented conflict with Katori or Ye: my collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) are not clock projects, and as an experimentalist I am only field-adjacent to precision measurement. I no longer propose B019, so my earlier note on proximity to the IceCube community no longer affects my configuration. I support recording Johansson's recusal on B042 and noting Kroll's Boulder stay for the final ballot. I judge neither to change the weight of their stated positions on the candidates I propose, and as Chair I will not let any of this affect procedure.
